title: What anointing does (CCC 1520–1523)
hookLine: strength, peace, courage, union with Christ's suffering

lines: OIL ON THE FOREHEAD AND HANDS.
cards: A hospital room, late afternoon, the television muted. The woman in the bed has surgery tomorrow morning. A priest comes in with a small metal case, the size of a lipstick.
He prays, lays his hands on her head in silence, then traces oil with his thumb on her forehead and the palms of her hands. Nothing about the surgery changes. So what just happened?
Some people think this sacrament is only for the last hour of life. The Catechism tells a wider story.

teach.h: IS ANY MAN SICK AMONG YOU?
teach.b: Back on day one hundred thirty, you met its old name, extreme unction, and learned it isn't only for the dying. Today, what it does.

The roots are in the letter of James, in the Douay-Rheims: "Is any man sick among you? Let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord."
Not a dying man alone: a sick person who calls the community in. The Catechism names the gifts.
First, a gift of the Holy Spirit: strength, peace and courage to face serious illness or the frailty of old age. Not a guaranteed cure.
Healing of the body can come, it says, if God wills it, but the first gift is inward: the strength not to be swallowed by fear or discouragement.
Second, union with Christ's own suffering. Catholic teaching says the sick person, joined to Christ, can find their suffering takes on a new meaning. It isn't wasted.
Paul tells the Colossians he rejoices in his sufferings, filling up in his flesh what is lacking in Christ's sufferings, for the sake of the Church.

teach.h: A GIFT FOR THE WHOLE CHURCH.
teach.b: Third, a gift for the Church. The sick person isn't only receiving: joined to Christ's suffering, they contribute to the good of the whole people of God, and the Church prays for them in return.
Fourth, for those near the end, a preparation for the last journey, completing the anointings that marked a whole Christian life, from baptism on. So the oil didn't move the surgery.
It was meant to change who walks into it.

how: Catholics who are seriously ill, facing major surgery, or weakened by old age can ask a priest for the anointing of the sick, which can take place at home, in a hospital, or during a parish Mass for the sick.

games.why: the Catechism speaks of serious illness and old age. its first gift is strength, peace and courage.

practice: Bring to mind one person who is ill, or frail, or waiting on a diagnosis, and picture where they are right now: a bed, a waiting room, a kitchen chair. Think of one plain thing you could say to them that isn't advice.
If you pray, ask God to give them strength, peace and courage; if you don't, just hold them in mind.

wordCard.voice: What anointing does. Strength, peace and courage in illness, union with Christ's suffering, a gift for the whole Church, and for some, a preparation for the last journey. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: olive oil, the oil of the anointing in James 5:14.

carryVoice: Your line: strength in sickness. The oil is for the frightened, not only the dying. Until tomorrow.
